title: Define programming paradigm and name any two programming paradigms other than OOP.
chunks: A programming paradigm is a fundamental style or approach to programming, dictating how tasks are structured and executed. Two other paradigms besides Object-Oriented Programming (OOP) are: Procedural Programming (e.g., C) Functional Programming (e.g., Haskell, LISP)

title: When was Java officially announced by Sun Microsystems, and what was its original name?
chunks: Java was officially announced by Sun Microsystems in 1995 . Its original name during development was Oak (named after an oak tree outside James Gosling's office).

title: Define Object-Oriented Programming and list the six pillars of OOP.
chunks: Object-Oriented Programming (OOP) is a paradigm centered around "objects" (which contain data in the form of fields and code in the form of methods) rather than "actions" or logic. The six pillars (or core concepts) of OOP are: Class Object Encapsulation Abstraction Inheritance Polymorphism

title: Differentiate between a class and an object with one suitable example.
chunks: Class Object A logical template or blueprint. A physical entity/instance created from a class. Does not allocate memory when created. Allocates memory in the heap when instantiated. Declared using the class keyword. Created using the new keyword. Example: If Car is a class (the blueprint), then a Red Tesla Model S is an object (an actual car).

title: Define encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance, and polymorphism.
chunks: Encapsulation: Wrapping data (variables) and code (methods) together into a single unit (class), protecting the data from outside interference. Abstraction: Hiding internal implementation details and exposing only the necessary functionalities to the user. Inheritance: A mechanism where a new class (child) inherits properties and behaviors from an existing class (parent), promoting code reusability. Polymorphism: The ability of a single entity (method, object, or operator) to take on multiple forms and behave differently based on the context.

title: What is the difference between procedural and object-oriented programming?
chunks: Procedural Programming (POP) Object-Oriented Programming (OOP) Program is divided into small parts called functions . Program is divided into parts called objects . Follows a Top-Down approach. Follows a Bottom-Up approach. Data is freely moving and less secure. Data is hidden (encapsulated) and highly secure. Example: C, Pascal Example: Java, C++, Python

title: What are JDK, JRE, and JVM?
chunks: JDK (Java Development Kit): A full software development environment. It contains the JRE plus development tools like the compiler ( javac ) and debugger. JRE (Java Runtime Environment): The environment required to run Java programs. It contains the JVM and core class libraries. JVM (Java Virtual Machine): An abstract machine that executes Java Bytecode. It makes Java platform-independent.

title: What is bytecode, and why is Java considered platform-independent?
chunks: Bytecode is a highly optimized set of instructions generated by the Java compiler ( javac ) after compiling the source code. It is not machine code, but rather intermediate code. Java is platform-independent because the compiler generates this bytecode instead of native machine code. This bytecode can be executed on any operating system as long as that system has a JVM (Java Virtual Machine) installed to interpret it (Write Once, Run Anywhere).

title: What is a Java package? Give two examples of commonly used packages.
chunks: A Java package is a mechanism for organizing related classes and interfaces into a single namespace. It prevents naming conflicts and controls access (encapsulation). Two Examples: java.util (Contains utility classes like Scanner, ArrayList) java.lang (Contains core classes like String, Math. It is imported automatically)

title: List the four access modifiers in Java and state the default access level.
chunks: The four access modifiers in Java (from most restrictive to least) are: private (accessible only within the same class) default (no keyword; accessible only within the same package) protected (accessible within the same package and subclasses in other packages) public (accessible from anywhere) If no modifier is specified, the access level is default (package-private).

title: What is a class and what is an object in Java? Give one difference between them.
chunks: A class is a user-defined blueprint or prototype from which objects are created. An object is a runtime instance of a class that has state and behavior. Difference: A class is a logical entity that consumes no memory upon declaration, whereas an object is a physical entity that consumes memory space in the heap when instantiated.

title: What is the purpose of the new keyword in Java? Where is the newly created object stored?
chunks: The new keyword in Java is used to create a new object or array by allocating memory at runtime. It essentially instantiates a class. Storage: The newly created object is always stored in the Heap memory.

title: What is the difference between an instance variable and a local variable? State any two differences.
chunks: Instance Variable Local Variable Declared inside a class but outside any method. Declared inside a method, constructor, or block. Gets a default value (e.g., 0 for int) if not initialized. Does not get a default value; must be initialized before use.

title: What is a constructor in Java? State any two rules of a constructor.
chunks: A constructor is a special block of code that is called automatically when an object is instantiated. It is used to initialize the state of the object. Rules: The constructor name must exactly match the class name. A constructor must not have an explicit return type (not even void ).

title: What is constructor overloading? On what basis does the compiler distinguish overloaded constructors?
chunks: Constructor Overloading is a technique of having more than one constructor in a class with different parameter lists. It allows objects to be initialized in different ways. The compiler distinguishes them based on the number of parameters , the types of the parameters , and the order of the parameters .

title: What is constructor chaining? Name the two keywords used for constructor chaining.
chunks: Constructor chaining is the process of calling one constructor from another constructor with respect to the current object. It helps avoid duplicate code. The two keywords used are: this() : Used to call a constructor of the same class. super() : Used to call a constructor of the superclass (parent class).

title: What is the purpose of the this keyword in Java? State any two uses.
chunks: The this keyword is a reference variable that refers to the current object on which the method or constructor is being invoked. Two Uses: To resolve shadowing when instance variables and local parameters share the same name (e.g., this.name = name; ). To invoke another constructor in the same class (using this() ).

title: What is Garbage Collection in Java? When does an object become eligible for garbage collection?
chunks: Garbage Collection (GC) is the process by which Java programs perform automatic memory management, freeing up the heap by deleting objects that are no longer in use. An object becomes eligible for garbage collection when it is completely unreferenced (i.e., no live thread can access it). This happens if its reference is set to null , if it is created anonymously, or if references are reassigned.

title: What is autoboxing and unboxing in Java?
chunks: Autoboxing: The automatic conversion that the Java compiler makes between the primitive types and their corresponding object wrapper classes (e.g., converting int to Integer ). Unboxing: The reverse process; converting an object of a wrapper type back to its corresponding primitive value (e.g., converting Integer to int ).

title: What is String immutability? State one benefit of immutable Strings.
chunks: String immutability means that once a String object is created, its value or state cannot be changed. Any operation that alters the string creates a brand new String object rather than modifying the original. Benefit: It makes Strings thread-safe and allows caching in the String Constant Pool, which saves memory.

title: Define inheritance. List the different types of inheritance supported in Java.
chunks: Inheritance is a mechanism where a new class acquires the properties and methods of an existing class, establishing an IS-A relationship and promoting code reuse. Types supported in Java (via classes): Single Inheritance Multilevel Inheritance Hierarchical Inheritance (Note: Multiple and Hybrid inheritance are not supported through classes, only through interfaces).

title: What is the purpose of the super keyword? List any two uses.
chunks: The super keyword is a reference variable used to refer to the immediate parent class object. Two Uses: To invoke the immediate parent class constructor (e.g., super(); ). To invoke an overridden method in the parent class (e.g., super.display(); ).

title: What is the Object class? Name any two methods of the Object class.
chunks: The Object class (located in the java.lang package) is the root class of the Java class hierarchy. Every class in Java directly or indirectly inherits from the Object class. Two Methods: toString() equals(Object obj)

title: Define method overloading and method overriding.
chunks: Method Overloading: Creating multiple methods in the same class with the same name but different parameters (compile-time polymorphism). Method Overriding: Providing a specific implementation in a subclass for a method that is already defined in its parent class. The method signature must be identical (run-time polymorphism).

title: What is polymorphism? Name its two types.
chunks: Polymorphism is the ability of an object or method to take on many forms, allowing the same interface to be used for different underlying forms (data types). Two Types: Compile-time Polymorphism (Static binding, e.g., Method Overloading). Run-time Polymorphism (Dynamic binding, e.g., Method Overriding).

title: What is dynamic binding? Why is it also called late binding?
chunks: Dynamic Binding is the process where the compiler does not resolve the method call at compile time, but rather the JVM determines the actual method implementation to execute at runtime based on the actual object type. It is called late binding because the binding of the method call to the method body is delayed until the program is actually executing.

title: Define upcasting and downcasting in Java.
chunks: Upcasting: Casting a subclass reference variable to a superclass reference. This is done automatically and implicitly by the compiler. Downcasting: Casting a superclass reference variable back to a subclass reference. This must be done explicitly by the programmer and requires checking to prevent ClassCastException .

title: What is the purpose of the instanceof operator?
chunks: The instanceof operator is a binary operator used to test whether a given object is an instance of a specific class, subclass, or interface. It returns true or false . It is primarily used to check object types before attempting a downcast , preventing runtime exceptions.

title: What is an abstract class? What is an interface?
chunks: Abstract Class: A class declared with the abstract keyword that cannot be instantiated. It can contain both abstract methods (without a body) and concrete methods. Interface: A completely "abstract class" that acts as a contract. In modern Java, it primarily contains abstract methods and static constants, though it can now have default methods. A class implements an interface.

title: What are generics in Java? Give one example of a generic type parameter.
chunks: Generics enable types (classes and interfaces) to be parameters when defining classes, interfaces and methods. This provides stronger type checks at compile time and removes the need for explicit casting. Example: <T> is a generic type parameter where T stands for Type. Example usage: List<String> list = new ArrayList<String>();

title: Explain the Top-Down and Bottom-Up approaches with a suitable example.
chunks: Top-Down Approach: The problem is broken down into smaller sub-problems. It focuses on the main algorithm first, then the details (used in Procedural Programming like C). Example: Building a car by first designing the full car, then breaking it down into engine, wheels, and doors. Bottom-Up Approach: The smaller modules or objects are designed first, and then integrated together to form the complete system (used in Object-Oriented Programming like Java). Example: Designing the engine, wheels, and doors first as independent objects, then assembling them to build the car.

title: Explain how Java evolved from Oak and mention any three important features of Java.
chunks: Java was originally developed by James Gosling at Sun Microsystems in 1991 for interactive television and consumer electronics. It was initially named Oak . It was later renamed Java in 1995 and shifted focus to the World Wide Web because of its platform independence. Three Important Features: Platform Independent: Write once, run anywhere (WORA) using Bytecode and JVM. Object-Oriented: Everything is an object; follows OOP principles strictly. Robust & Secure: Strong memory management, automatic garbage collection, and no explicit pointers.

title: Explain the role of JDK, JRE, and JVM in executing a Java program.
chunks: JDK (Java Development Kit): The complete toolbox for a developer. It provides the compiler ( javac ) which translates the .java source code into a .class file (bytecode). JRE (Java Runtime Environment): The environment where the Java program runs. It provides the core class libraries and packages required for execution. JVM (Java Virtual Machine): The core engine inside the JRE. It reads the bytecode line by line, interprets it, and executes it on the host operating system.

title: Explain the basic structure of a Java program and write the standard main() method signature.
chunks: A basic Java program consists of a class definition containing methods. The entry point of any standalone Java application is the main method. public class HelloWorld { public static void main(String[] args) { System.out.println("Hello, World!"); } } public : Accessible from anywhere. static : Can be called without instantiating the class. void : Returns nothing. String[] args : Command-line arguments.

title: Explain Java identifiers, naming rules, comments, and the importance of proper coding conventions.
chunks: Identifiers: Names given to classes, variables, and methods. Rules: Must start with a letter, _ , or $ . Cannot be a keyword. Case-sensitive. Comments: Used to explain code. Single-line ( // ) and Multi-line ( /* ... */ ). Coding Conventions: Classes: PascalCase Methods/Variables: camelCase Constants: UPPER_SNAKE_CASE Importance: Improves code readability, maintainability, and collaboration among developers.

title: Explain built-in and user-defined packages with suitable examples. Also explain the purpose of the import statement.
chunks: Built-in Packages: Provided by the Java API. Example: java.util , java.io . User-defined Packages: Created by the programmer to group related classes. Example: package com.mycompany.utils; Import Statement: Used to bring a class or an entire package into visibility so it can be used without typing its fully qualified name (e.g., import java.util.Scanner; ).

title: Explain the four access modifiers in Java with respect to their accessibility.
chunks: Modifier Same Class Same Package Subclass (Diff Pkg) Diff Pkg (Non-subclass) Private Yes No No No Default Yes Yes No No Protected Yes Yes Yes No Public Yes Yes Yes Yes

title: Differentiate between variable scope and lifetime. Also explain dynamic initialization.
chunks: Scope: The region of the code where a variable is visible and accessible (e.g., block scope, method scope). Lifetime: The duration of time a variable exists in memory during program execution. Dynamic Initialization: Initializing a variable at runtime using an expression or method call, rather than a hardcoded constant. Example: double c = Math.sqrt(a*a + b*b);

title: Explain Java data types and differentiate between primitive and reference data types.
chunks: Primitive Data Types: Predefined by Java and hold actual values. There are 8: byte, short, int, long, float, double, char, boolean . They are stored in stack memory and have a fixed size. Reference Data Types: User-defined (except Arrays and Strings) and hold references (memory addresses) to the actual objects. They are stored in heap memory. Examples: Classes, Interfaces, Arrays.

title: Explain one-dimensional and two-dimensional arrays, and differentiate between for, while, and do-while loops.
chunks: Arrays: 1D Array: A linear list of elements. int[] arr = new int[5]; 2D Array: An array of arrays (a matrix). int[][] matrix = new int[3][3]; Loops: for: Used when the number of iterations is known in advance. while: Used when iterations are unknown; condition is checked before execution (entry-controlled). do-while: Condition is checked after execution (exit-controlled); guarantees execution at least once.

title: Explain the difference between stack and heap memory in Java with respect to object creation and references.
chunks: Heap Memory: This is where all actual objects and instance variables are stored. It is dynamically allocated at runtime when the new keyword is used. It is managed by the Garbage Collector. Stack Memory: This is where all local variables, method calls, and object references are stored. When you write Car c = new Car(); , the object itself goes in the heap, but the reference variable c is kept in the stack, pointing to the heap memory address.

title: Explain the default values of instance variables for int, double, char, boolean, and object reference types.
chunks: When instance variables are not explicitly initialized, Java assigns them default values: int (and byte, short, long): 0 double (and float): 0.0 char : '\u0000' (null character) boolean : false Object References (String, arrays, custom classes): null

title: Explain default/no-argument and parameterized constructors with suitable examples.
chunks: Default / No-Argument Constructor: Takes no parameters. If no constructor is defined, the compiler provides one automatically. Used for default initialization. class Box { Box() { System.out.println("Empty box created"); } } Parameterized Constructor: Takes parameters to initialize the object with specific values upon creation. class Box { int size; Box(int s) { this.size = s; } }

title: Explain constructor overloading with a suitable Java example.
chunks: Constructor Overloading allows a class to have multiple constructors with different parameter lists, giving flexibility in how an object is initialized. class Rectangle { int length, width; // Constructor 1: Default (Square) Rectangle() { length = 5; width = 5; } // Constructor 2: Parameterized Rectangle(int l, int w) { length = l; width = w; } }

title: Differentiate between constructor overloading and constructor chaining. Also mention the keywords used for constructor chaining.
chunks: Constructor Overloading: Having multiple separate constructors in the same class to handle different initialization scenarios. Constructor Chaining: The process where one constructor explicitly calls another constructor (either within the same class or from the parent class) to reuse initialization logic. Keywords for Chaining: this() - Calls another constructor in the same class. super() - Calls a constructor in the parent class.

title: Explain any three uses of the this keyword with suitable examples.
chunks: Resolve Shadowing: Used to distinguish instance variables from local parameters. this.name = name; Constructor Chaining: Used to invoke another constructor in the same class. this(10); // Calls parameterized constructor Pass as Argument: Used to pass the current object as a parameter to another method. helper.printDetails(this);

title: Explain private, default, protected, and public access modifiers in Java.
chunks: Private: The most restrictive. Accessible only within the class where it is declared. Used for data hiding. Default: (No keyword). Accessible only by classes within the same package. Protected: Accessible within the same package, and by subclasses located in other packages. Public: The least restrictive. Accessible from any class anywhere in the program.

title: Explain the Character wrapper class and any four useful methods of the Character class.
chunks: The Character class (in java.lang ) wraps a primitive char value in an object. It provides numerous utility methods for character manipulation. Four Useful Methods: Character.isLetter(ch) : Returns true if the character is a letter. Character.isDigit(ch) : Returns true if the character is a number. Character.isUpperCase(ch) : Returns true if the character is uppercase. Character.toLowerCase(ch) : Converts the character to lowercase.

title: Explain the two ways of creating a String in Java: using a string literal and using the new keyword.
chunks: String Literal: String s = "Hello"; The JVM first checks the String Constant Pool . If "Hello" exists, it returns the reference. If not, it creates it. This is highly memory-efficient. new Keyword: String s = new String("Hello"); The JVM forces the creation of a brand new String object in the Heap memory, bypassing the pool entirely, even if "Hello" already exists in the pool.

title: Differentiate between = = and equals() when comparing String objects with a suitable example.
chunks: == Operator: Compares the memory references (addresses) of two objects to see if they point to the exact same object in memory. equals() Method: Compares the actual contents/values of the two objects for logical equality. String s1 = new String("Java"); String s2 = new String("Java"); System.out.println(s1 == s2); // false (different heap objects) System.out.println(s1.equals(s2)); // true (same content)

title: Explain single, multilevel, hierarchical, and hybrid inheritance with suitable examples.
chunks: Single: Class B inherits from Class A. (Dog inherits Animal) Multilevel: Class C inherits from Class B, which inherits from Class A. (Puppy inherits Dog inherits Animal) Hierarchical: Multiple classes inherit from a single Class A. (Dog and Cat both inherit Animal) Hybrid: A combination of two or more types. In Java, true hybrid inheritance involving multiple parents is only achievable via Interfaces to avoid the Diamond Problem.

title: Explain the three major uses of the super keyword with suitable examples.
chunks: Invoke Parent Constructor: super(); (Must be the first line in the child constructor). Invoke Parent Method: Used when the child has overridden the method. super.display(); Access Parent Variable: Used when the child class hides a parent's variable with the same name. System.out.println(super.x);

title: Explain the Object class and the purpose of toString(), equals(), hashCode(), and getClass().
chunks: The Object class is the universal superclass of all Java classes. toString() : Returns a string representation of the object (often overridden to show field values). equals() : Used to compare the logical equality of two objects. hashCode() : Returns an integer hash code value for the object, crucial for collections like HashMap . getClass() : Returns the runtime class object of the current instance (used in reflection).

title: Differentiate between method overloading and method overriding with suitable examples.
chunks: Method Overloading Method Overriding Occurs within the same class . Occurs between parent and child classes. Parameters must be different. Parameters must be exactly the same. Resolved at Compile-Time (Static Binding). Resolved at Run-Time (Dynamic Binding). Example: add(int a, int b) vs add(double a, double b) Example: Animal.sound() overridden by Dog.sound()

title: Differentiate between compile-time and run-time polymorphism in Java.
chunks: Compile-time Polymorphism: Achieved through Method Overloading. The compiler knows exactly which method to call based on the method signature (number and type of arguments). Fast execution because binding happens early. Run-time Polymorphism: Achieved through Method Overriding. A parent reference points to a child object. The JVM determines which overridden method to execute during runtime based on the actual object type , not the reference type.

title: Explain dynamic binding and object casting with reference to upcasting and downcasting.
chunks: Dynamic Binding is resolving a method call at runtime depending on the actual object. Upcasting: Casting a subclass to a superclass. It is automatic. Animal a = new Dog(); This triggers dynamic binding when overridden methods are called. Downcasting: Casting a superclass back to a subclass. It must be explicit. Dog d = (Dog) a; This is needed to access methods specific only to the child class.

title: Explain the instanceof operator and its importance before performing downcasting.
chunks: The instanceof operator checks if an object is an instance of a specific class or interface. Importance in Downcasting: Downcasting a parent reference to a child reference is dangerous because if the parent reference doesn't actually hold that specific child object, the JVM throws a ClassCastException . Using if (obj instanceof Dog) { Dog d = (Dog) obj; } ensures the downcast is mathematically safe.

title: Differentiate between an abstract class and an interface. Also state how interfaces support multiple inheritance.
chunks: Abstract Class Interface Can have both abstract and concrete methods. Historically only abstract methods (now allows default methods). Can have state (instance variables). Only public static final constants. A class can extend only one abstract class. A class can implement multiple interfaces. Multiple Inheritance: Java prevents a class from extending multiple classes to avoid ambiguity, but it allows a class to implement multiple interfaces because interfaces (traditionally) have no implementation to clash.

title: Explain generics and their advantages. What do the type parameters T, E, K, and V represent?
chunks: Generics allow classes, interfaces, and methods to operate on specified data types as parameters, providing compile-time type safety. Advantages: Prevents ClassCastException at runtime and eliminates the need for manual type-casting. Common Parameters: T : Type (General) E : Element (Used heavily in Collections like ArrayList) K : Key (Used in Maps) V : Value (Used in Maps)

title: Explain ArrayList and packages in Java. Mention common operations of ArrayList and the purpose of packages.
chunks: ArrayList: A resizable-array implementation of the List interface found in java.util . Unlike standard arrays, it grows and shrinks dynamically. Common Operations: add() , remove() , get() , size() . Packages: Containers that group related classes and interfaces together. Purpose: To prevent naming conflicts, group related code logically, and control access visibility (via package-private modifiers).

title: Compare procedural programming and OOP with respect to approach, data handling, security, reusability, inheritance, and polymorphism.
chunks: Feature Procedural Programming Object-Oriented Programming Approach Top-Down approach. Bottom-Up approach. Data Handling Data moves freely between functions globally. Data is tied to objects and controlled via methods. Security Low security (no access modifiers). High security (data hiding via encapsulation & modifiers). Reusability Low (code duplication is common). High (achieved via Inheritance and objects). Inheritance Not supported. Supported (Single, Multilevel, Hierarchical). Polymorphism Not supported. Supported (Overloading, Overriding).

title: Explain the six pillars of OOP—class, object, encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance, and polymorphism—with suitable examples.
chunks: Class: A blueprint for creating objects. Ex: A Vehicle class defining speed and color. Object: A real-world instance of a class. Ex: A specific red Ferrari. Encapsulation: Wrapping data and methods into a single unit to protect the data. Ex: A capsule containing medicine; private variables accessed via getters/setters. Abstraction: Hiding complex implementation details and showing only essentials. Ex: Driving a car without knowing how the internal combustion engine works. Inheritance: A child class acquiring properties from a parent class. Ex: Dog inherits from Animal . Polymorphism: One entity taking many forms. Ex: A sound() method that barks for a Dog but meows for a Cat.

title: Explain Java's platform independence in detail, from source code compilation to bytecode execution through the JVM.
chunks: Java's "Write Once, Run Anywhere" capability relies on its two-step execution process: Compilation: The developer writes Program.java (Source Code). The Java Compiler ( javac ) compiles this into Program.class . Instead of compiling it into machine-specific code (like C++), it compiles it into Bytecode . This bytecode is entirely independent of the underlying OS or hardware. Execution: The compiled bytecode is transported to any machine (Windows, Mac, Linux). That machine must have a JVM (Java Virtual Machine) installed. The JVM reads the bytecode and translates it into the specific machine-level instructions native to that exact operating system. Therefore, while the JVM is platform- dependent , the Java program (bytecode) itself is totally platform- independent .

title: Write a Java program containing a class, instance variables, constructor, method, and objects. Explain the execution of the program.
chunks: class Car { String model; // Instance variable // Constructor Car(String m) { model = m; } // Method void display() { System.out.println("Car Model: " + model); } } public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) { Car c1 = new Car("Tesla"); // Object creation c1.display(); // Method invocation } } Execution: The JVM enters the main method. It encounters the new keyword, which allocates heap memory for a Car object. The constructor Car("Tesla") is called, initializing the model instance variable to "Tesla". Finally, the display() method is invoked on the c1 object, printing the output to the console.

title: Explain Java packages and access modifiers. Write a suitable program demonstrating private, default, protected, and public members.
chunks: Packages group related classes to avoid name clashes. Access Modifiers control the visibility of classes and members. package mypack; public class AccessDemo { private int priv = 1; // Only this class int def = 2; // Only this package protected int prot = 3; // This package + subclasses public int pub = 4; // Everywhere public void show() { System.out.println(priv + def + prot + pub); } }

title: Explain Java data types, arrays, and operators with suitable examples. Evaluate the expression 5 + 3 * 2 % 4 using operator precedence.
chunks: Data Types: Primitives ( int x = 5; ) and References ( String s = "Hi"; ). Arrays: Homogeneous collections. int[] arr = {1, 2, 3}; Operators: Arithmetic ( + , - ), Relational ( > , == ), Logical ( && , || ). Evaluation of 5 + 3 * 2 % 4 : Precedence of * and % is higher than + . They evaluate left-to-right. 3 * 2 = 6 6 % 4 = 2 (Remainder of 6 divided by 4) 5 + 2 = 7

title: Write a Java program to create a Book class with title and price fields. Create two objects with different values and display their details.
chunks: class Book { String title; double price; Book(String t, double p) { title = t; price = p; } void display() { System.out.println("Title: " + title + ", Price: $" + price); } } public class Library { public static void main(String[] args) { Book b1 = new Book("Java Complete Reference", 45.99); Book b2 = new Book("Head First Java", 35.50); b1.display(); b2.display(); } }

title: Write a Java program using an array and loops to calculate the average marks of five students.
chunks: public class AverageMarks { public static void main(String[] args) { int[] marks = {85, 90, 78, 92, 88}; int sum = 0; for (int i = 0; i < marks.length; i++) { sum += marks[i]; } double average = (double) sum / marks.length; System.out.println("Average Marks: " + average); } }

title: Explain Java control statements with suitable examples of if-else, switch-case, loops, break, continue, and the ternary operator.
chunks: if-else: Branching based on a boolean. if(x > 0) { ... } else { ... } switch-case: Multi-way branch. switch(day) { case 1: ... break; } loops: Repeating code. for(int i=0; i<5; i++) { ... } break: Exits the entire loop or switch immediately. continue: Skips the current iteration and proceeds to the next iteration of the loop. Ternary Operator: A one-line if-else. int max = (a > b) ? a : b;

title: Write a Java program that uses an array, loop, and conditional statement to count negative numbers and display the result.
chunks: public class NegativeCounter { public static void main(String[] args) { int[] numbers = {5, -2, 9, -8, 0, -1, 3}; int count = 0; for(int num : numbers) { if(num < 0) { count++; } } System.out.println("Total negative numbers: " + count); } }

title: Explain Classes and Objects in Java in detail. Describe how objects are created using new, how multiple objects of the same class maintain independent instance variables, and illustrate with a suitable example.
chunks: A Class is a blueprint. An Object is a physical instance. The new keyword allocates distinct heap memory for every object created. Because each object gets its own memory block in the heap, they maintain independent copies of instance variables . Changing the variable in one object does not affect the other. class Account { int balance; } public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) { Account acc1 = new Account(); Account acc2 = new Account(); acc1.balance = 500; acc2.balance = 1000; // acc1 and acc2 are independent. } }

title: Explain instance variables and local variables in Java. Discuss their declaration, default/initialization requirements, lifetime, and memory behavior with suitable examples.
chunks: Property Instance Variable Local Variable Declaration Inside class, outside methods. Inside a method or block. Memory Stored in the Heap (inside the object). Stored in the Stack . Lifetime Lives as long as the object lives. Destroyed when the method execution completes. Initialization Automatically initialized to defaults (0, null). NO default value. Must be explicitly initialized.

title: Explain constructors in Java in detail. Discuss constructor rules, default/no-argument constructor, parameterized constructor, and the role of constructors in object initialization.
chunks: Constructors are special blocks invoked when an object is instantiated via new . Rules: Must have the exact same name as the class. Cannot have a return type. Role: They allocate default or specific values to instance variables the moment the object is born, ensuring the object starts in a valid state. title: Explain Garbage Collection and finalization in Java. Discuss different situations in which an object becomes eligible for GC, the role of finalize(), why finalize() is deprecated, and modern alternatives such as try-with-resources and Cleaner.

Deprecation: finalize() was deprecated in Java 9 because it is unpredictable, impacts performance, and can cause memory leaks if implemented poorly. Modern Alternatives: Use try-with-resources (implementing AutoCloseable ) for deterministic resource cleanup, or the java.lang.ref.Cleaner API.

title: Create a form with a TextField and a Button that displays the entered name in a Label.

Program Implementation import java.awt.*; import java.awt.event.*; public class GreetingForm extends Frame implements ActionListener { private TextField txtName; private Button btnSubmit; private Label lblResult; public GreetingForm() { // Configure Frame window setTitle("User Greeting Application"); setLayout(new FlowLayout(FlowLayout.CENTER, 15, 15)); // Initialize UI components Label lblPrompt = new Label("Enter Your Name:"); txtName = new TextField(20); btnSubmit = new Button("Submit"); lblResult = new Label("Result will appear here..."); // Register event listener btnSubmit.addActionListener(this); // Add window closing listener to handle exit addWindowListener(new WindowAdapter() { @Override public void windowClosing(WindowEvent we) { System.exit(0); } }); // Add components to the frame container add(lblPrompt); add(txtName); add(btnSubmit); add(lblResult); setSize(400, 180); setLocationRelativeTo(null); setVisible(true); } @Override public void actionPerformed(ActionEvent e) { String enteredName = txtName.getText().trim(); if (enteredName.isEmpty()) { lblResult.setForeground(Color.RED); lblResult.setText("Error: Name field cannot be blank!"); } else { lblResult.setForeground(new Color(16, 185, 129)); lblResult.setText("Hello, " + enteredName + "! Welcome to Java GUI."); } } public static void main(String[] args) { new GreetingForm(); } }

Technical Architecture & Event Flow Component Roles: TextField acts as the user data entry source, Button acts as the action event generator, and Label functions as the passive visual recipient. Delegation Event Model: Calling btnSubmit.addActionListener(this) registers the enclosing class as an observer. When clicked, the Event Dispatch Thread (EDT) invokes actionPerformed() . Input Sanitization: The method trim() eliminates stray whitespace, preventing false submissions of empty characters. Lifecycle Termination: A WindowAdapter intercepts the native OS close box click to cleanly shut down the JVM via System.exit(0) .

title: Write a GUI program with two Checkboxes for selecting hobbies and display the selected choices.
chunks: This program demonstrates how to handle multiple independent binary selections using Checkbox components and an ItemListener in Java AWT.

Program Implementation import java.awt.*; import java.awt.event.*; public class HobbySelector extends Frame implements ItemListener { private Checkbox cbReading; private Checkbox cbSports; private Label lblStatus; public HobbySelector() { setTitle("Hobby Selection Portal"); setLayout(new GridLayout(4, 1, 10, 10)); Label lblTitle = new Label("Select Your Hobbies:", Label.CENTER); cbReading = new Checkbox("Reading Books"); cbSports = new Checkbox("Outdoor Sports"); lblStatus = new Label("Selected: None", Label.CENTER); // Register ItemListener on both checkboxes cbReading.addItemListener(this); cbSports.addItemListener(this); add(lblTitle); add(cbReading); add(cbSports); add(lblStatus); addWindowListener(new WindowAdapter() { @Override public void windowClosing(WindowEvent e) { System.exit(0); } }); setSize(360, 220); setLocationRelativeTo(null); setVisible(true); } @Override public void itemStateChanged(ItemEvent e) { StringBuilder selected = new StringBuilder(); if (cbReading.getState()) { selected.append("Reading Books; "); } if (cbSports.getState()) { selected.append("Outdoor Sports; "); } if (selected.length() == 0) { lblStatus.setText("Selected: None"); } else { lblStatus.setText("Selected: " + selected.toString()); } } public static void main(String[] args) { new HobbySelector(); } }

Technical Highlights & Event Mechanics Non-Exclusive Selection: Unlike radio buttons, standalone Checkbox instances allow users to choose none, either, or both hobbies concurrently. ItemListener Interface: Handles state change notifications via itemStateChanged(ItemEvent e) whenever a box is toggled. State Inspection: Calling cb.getState() returns a primitive boolean ( true if selected, false if unselected). Dynamic String Construction: StringBuilder efficiently aggregates active selections without producing unnecessary intermediate String garbage on the heap. Expected Execution Behavior: When the user checks 'Reading Books', the status label updates to 'Selected: Reading Books; '. Toggling 'Outdoor Sports' appends it. Unchecking both resets the label to 'Selected: None'.

Program Implementation import java.awt.*; import java.awt.event.*; public class CourseRadioDemo extends Frame implements ItemListener { private CheckboxGroup courseGroup; private Checkbox rbJava, rbPython, rbCpp; private Label lblResult; public CourseRadioDemo() { setTitle("Degree Specialization Selector"); setLayout(new GridLayout(5, 1, 8, 8)); Label lblPrompt = new Label("Choose your primary engineering track:"); // CheckboxGroup enforces mutual exclusion across grouped buttons courseGroup = new CheckboxGroup(); rbJava = new Checkbox("Java Enterprise Programming", courseGroup, false); rbPython = new Checkbox("Python Artificial Intelligence", courseGroup, false); rbCpp = new Checkbox("C++ Systems Architecture", courseGroup, false); lblResult = new Label("Selected Track: None", Label.CENTER); // Register ItemListener on each option rbJava.addItemListener(this); rbPython.addItemListener(this); rbCpp.addItemListener(this); add(lblPrompt); add(rbJava); add(rbPython); add(rbCpp); add(lblResult); addWindowListener(new WindowAdapter() { @Override public void windowClosing(WindowEvent e) { System.exit(0); } }); setSize(400, 240); setLocationRelativeTo(null); setVisible(true); } @Override public void itemStateChanged(ItemEvent e) { Checkbox active = courseGroup.getSelectedCheckbox(); if (active != null) { lblResult.setText("Selected Track: " + active.getLabel()); } } public static void main(String[] args) { new CourseRadioDemo(); } }

Architectural Breakdown Radio Button Simulation: AWT lacks a dedicated JRadioButton class; passing a CheckboxGroup reference into the Checkbox(label, group, state) constructor renders the native circular radio button peer. Mutual Exclusion Enforcement: When any button inside the group is clicked, the group automatically clears all other members. Querying Active Option: courseGroup.getSelectedCheckbox() returns the active Checkbox reference, from which getLabel() retrieves the textual course name. Expected Execution Behavior: When a user clicks 'Python Artificial Intelligence', any previously selected course (e.g. Java) is deselected automatically. The status label immediately reflects the active choice.

title: Write a program that displays a message when the mouse enters and exits a component.

Program Implementation import java.awt.*; import java.awt.event.*; public class MouseBoundaryMonitor extends Frame implements MouseListener { private Panel sensorBox; private Label lblStatus; public MouseBoundaryMonitor() { setTitle("Mouse Boundary Monitor"); setLayout(new BorderLayout(10, 10)); sensorBox = new Panel(); sensorBox.setBackground(new Color(30, 41, 59)); // Slate background lblStatus = new Label("Status: Hover your mouse inside the dark box above", Label.CENTER); // Register listener with the target sensor panel sensorBox.addMouseListener(this); add(sensorBox, BorderLayout.CENTER); add(lblStatus, BorderLayout.SOUTH); addWindowListener(new WindowAdapter() { @Override public void windowClosing(WindowEvent e) { System.exit(0); } }); setSize(440, 260); setLocationRelativeTo(null); setVisible(true); } @Override public void mouseEntered(MouseEvent e) { sensorBox.setBackground(new Color(56, 189, 248)); // Sky blue highlight lblStatus.setText("Status: Mouse has ENTERED the panel boundary! (" + e.getX() + ", " + e.getY() + ")"); } @Override public void mouseExited(MouseEvent e) { sensorBox.setBackground(new Color(30, 41, 59)); // Restore slate lblStatus.setText("Status: Mouse has EXITED the panel boundary."); } // Required MouseListener methods satisfied with empty bodies public void mouseClicked(MouseEvent e) {} public void mousePressed(MouseEvent e) {} public void mouseReleased(MouseEvent e) {} public static void main(String[] args) { new MouseBoundaryMonitor(); } }

title: Write a program that displays a message dialog when a user clicks a button.
chunks: In Java AWT, modal alert popups are created using the java.awt.Dialog class. The program below launches a modal dialog upon clicking an alert button.

Program Implementation import java.awt.*; import java.awt.event.*; public class DialogDemo extends Frame implements ActionListener { private Button btnLaunch; public DialogDemo() { setTitle("AWT Dialog System"); setLayout(new FlowLayout(FlowLayout.CENTER, 25, 25)); btnLaunch = new Button("Launch Information Dialog"); btnLaunch.addActionListener(this); add(btnLaunch); addWindowListener(new WindowAdapter() { @Override public void windowClosing(WindowEvent e) { System.exit(0); } }); setSize(360, 160); setLocationRelativeTo(null); setVisible(true); } @Override public void actionPerformed(ActionEvent e) { // Construct modal dialog: parent Frame, Title, boolean modal Dialog infoDialog = new Dialog(this, "Alert Notification", true); infoDialog.setLayout(new FlowLayout(FlowLayout.CENTER, 15, 15)); Label lblMessage = new Label("System Alert: Operation completed successfully!"); Button btnDismiss = new Button("Acknowledge & Close"); btnDismiss.addActionListener(ae -> infoDialog.setVisible(false)); infoDialog.add(lblMessage); infoDialog.add(btnDismiss); infoDialog.setSize(300, 140); infoDialog.setLocationRelativeTo(this); infoDialog.setVisible(true); // Blocks until dismissed due to modality } public static void main(String[] args) { new DialogDemo(); } }

Modal vs Modeless Architecture Modal Dialogs: Passing true as the third argument constructs a modal dialog, preventing user interaction with all parent windows until closed. Event Blocking: The call infoDialog.setVisible(true) blocks further thread progression on that call stack until setVisible(false) or dispose() is invoked. Resource Disposal: Dismissing a dialog with dispose() frees native OS window handles. Modality Comparison: Passing false creates a modeless dialog where users can freely click back and forth between the popup and the parent window. Expected Execution Behavior: Clicking the launch button opens a compact 300x140 popup window centered on the main frame. The parent frame remains unresponsive until 'Acknowledge & Close' is pressed.

title: Write a basic Applet example that displays a message in paint() and identify where init() is used.
chunks: An Applet is an embeddable Java GUI component designed to execute within an external browser environment or the Applet Viewer utility.

Applet Code Implementation import java.applet.Applet; import java.awt.Graphics; import java.awt.Color; import java.awt.Font; /* <applet code="HelloApplet.class" width="400" height="180"> </applet> */ public class HelloApplet extends Applet { private String bannerText; // init() is invoked ONCE when the applet is first instantiated @Override public void init() { setBackground(new Color(15, 23, 42)); // Dark slate background bannerText = "Welcome to Java Applet Architecture!"; System.out.println("init() lifecycle hook executed: State initialized."); } // paint() is called whenever the screen canvas needs repainting @Override public void paint(Graphics g) { g.setColor(new Color(56, 189, 248)); // Cyan text g.setFont(new Font("SansSerif", Font.BOLD, 18)); g.drawString(bannerText, 30, 90); } }

The Role and Purpose of init() First Lifecycle Milestone: The init() method is the first method called by the browser runtime immediately after the applet class bytecode is loaded into memory. Initialization Tasks: It functions as the applet's conceptual constructor. Developers use it to parse HTML <param> tags, load fonts and images, create child AWT components, and set background/foreground palettes. Execution Frequency: Unlike start() and paint() which can execute multiple times whenever a browser tab is revisited or resized, init() is strictly guaranteed to execute only once per applet session. Lifecycle Transitions: The complete sequence is init() → start() → paint() . If the user navigates away or minimizes the browser, stop() pauses the applet. When the browser tab is closed, destroy() releases resources. Because applets inherit from java.awt.Panel , they support nested layouts, event listeners, and graphics rendering using double buffering to avoid screen flicker.

title: Compare FlowLayout and GridLayout for arranging six buttons. State which layout best matches a 2-by-3 button grid and why.
chunks: Arranging six push buttons presents distinct structural characteristics depending on whether FlowLayout or GridLayout is employed. Feature FlowLayout GridLayout(2, 3) Spatial Organization Sequential row placement left-to-right; wraps dynamically based on container width. Fixed rectangular mathematical matrix divided into equal rows and columns. Component Sizing Respects individual preferred size of each button (label length determines button width). Forces all buttons to uniform identical width and height regardless of text length. Window Resizing Behavior Unpredictable reflow: shrinking width reorganizes 6 buttons into 1x6, 3x2, or 6x1. Maintains strict 2-row by 3-column topology; scales cells proportionally. Gaps & Alignment Horizontal and vertical pixel gaps, aligned LEFT, CENTER, or RIGHT. Uniform horizontal and vertical pixel gaps between cells. Conclusion & Justification: GridLayout is unequivocally superior for a 2-by-3 button arrangement. new GridLayout(2, 3, 5, 5) guarantees a deterministic geometric matrix of exactly 2 rows and 3 columns that will never break or wrap onto stray lines during window resizing.

Layout Sizing Formula & Grid Mathematics In GridLayout(r, c) , the container calculates component bounds dynamically: cellWidth = (containerWidth - (c - 1) * hgap) / c and cellHeight = (containerHeight - (r - 1) * vgap) / r . This mathematical guarantee ensures that regardless of font sizes or label lengths, all six buttons remain perfectly symmetric, aligned, and proportional across screen resolutions. Furthermore, FlowLayout exhibits dynamic reflow: stretching the window displays all buttons in one horizontal line (1x6), whereas narrowing it forces buttons onto multiple rows (3x2 or 6x1). Only GridLayout(2, 3) preserves the user's mental model of a structured two-row matrix.

title: A button click does not update a label. Analyze two possible event-handling mistakes and suggest corrections.
chunks: When a button click fails to update a target label in Java AWT, the root cause invariably lies in a breakdown within the Delegation Event Model. The two most prevalent mistakes are analyzed below:

Mistake 1: Forgetting to Register the Listener with the Event Source Defect: The programmer creates the Button and defines the actionPerformed() method, but fails to call button.addActionListener(...) . Because no listener is registered in the button's internal observer list, clicks generate events that are discarded silently. // WRONG: Event generated but never dispatched Button btn = new Button("Submit"); // Missing: btn.addActionListener(this); // CORRECTION: Explicitly register the listener callback btn.addActionListener(this);

Mistake 2: Variable Shadowing / Scope Re-declaration Defect: The class declares an instance variable Label lblOutput , but the constructor re-declares a local variable Label lblOutput = new Label() . The local reference is added to the screen, while actionPerformed() modifies the unattached instance variable (or throws a NullPointerException ). public class DefectDemo extends Frame implements ActionListener { private Label lblOutput; // Instance field public DefectDemo() { // WRONG: 'Label' type re-declared locally, shadowing the instance field! Label lblOutput = new Label("Initial"); add(lblOutput); } public void actionPerformed(ActionEvent e) { // Modifies the NULL instance variable, NOT the screen component! lblOutput.setText("Updated!"); // Throws NullPointerException! } } // CORRECTION: Assign to instance field directly: lblOutput = new Label("Initial");

Mistake 3: Uncaught Runtime Exceptions Inside actionPerformed Defect: If an unhandled exception (such as NullPointerException or NumberFormatException ) occurs during event handling before reaching label.setText() , the execution aborts silently on the Event Dispatch Thread without updating the screen. Correction: Always enclose event-handling logic within robust try-catch blocks to log errors and guarantee GUI feedback.

title: Differentiate MouseListener and KeyListener and give one suitable use for each.
chunks: Both MouseListener and KeyListener belong to java.awt.event , but they intercept distinct hardware peripheral interactions: Dimension MouseListener KeyListener Event Source Peripheral Hardware mouse/pointing device. Physical or virtual alphanumeric keyboard. Dispatched Event Class java.awt.event.MouseEvent java.awt.event.KeyEvent Interface Methods 5 methods: mouseClicked() , mousePressed() , mouseReleased() , mouseEntered() , mouseExited() . 3 methods: keyTyped() , keyPressed() , keyReleased() . Corresponding Adapter Class java.awt.event.MouseAdapter java.awt.event.KeyAdapter Focus Requirement Does not require explicit input focus (triggers wherever pointer hovers/clicks). Requires the target component to possess active keyboard focus ( requestFocus() ). Suitable Real-World Use Cases: MouseListener: Interactive CAD/Drawing canvas where clicking captures mouse coordinates $(X, Y)$ via e.getX() , e.getY() to draw shapes. KeyListener: Hotkey navigation or real-time input sanitization (e.g., blocking non-numeric keystrokes in a PIN entry field).

Code Demonstration of Listener Contracts // MouseListener: Tracks mouse cursor coordinates and clicks component.addMouseListener(new MouseAdapter() { public void mouseClicked(MouseEvent e) { System.out.println("Mouse clicked at X=" + e.getX() + ", Y=" + e.getY()); } }); // KeyListener: Captures keyboard shortcuts and Enter key submissions component.addKeyListener(new KeyAdapter() { public void keyPressed(KeyEvent e) { if (e.getKeyCode() == KeyEvent.VK_ENTER) { System.out.println("Enter key shortcut triggered!"); } } }); MouseAdapter and KeyAdapter abstract classes provide empty default implementations, preventing code clutter from unused interface methods. Adapter Pattern Utility: Because MouseListener declares five abstract methods and KeyListener declares three, implementing them directly requires writing dummy empty bodies for unused methods. Java provides MouseAdapter and KeyAdapter abstract classes which define empty implementations, enabling developers to override only the specific events they care about. This adapter pattern greatly reduces boilerplate code in complex graphical user interfaces.

It divides space into five geographic zones: NORTH , SOUTH , EAST , WEST , and CENTER . import java.awt.*; import java.awt.event.*; public class FiveRegionBorderLayout extends Frame { public FiveRegionBorderLayout() { setTitle("BorderLayout: 5 Geographic Zones"); // Explicitly instantiate BorderLayout with 8px horizontal and vertical gaps setLayout(new BorderLayout(8, 8)); Button btnNorth = new Button("NORTH (Header Area)"); Button btnSouth = new Button("SOUTH (Footer Area)"); Button btnEast = new Button("EAST (Sidebar)"); Button btnWest = new Button("WEST (Navigation)"); Button btnCenter = new Button("CENTER (Main Workspace)"); // Set visual background colors to clearly distinguish regions btnNorth.setBackground(new Color(56, 189, 248)); btnSouth.setBackground(new Color(244, 114, 182)); btnEast.setBackground(new Color(129, 140, 248)); btnWest.setBackground(new Color(129, 140, 248)); btnCenter.setBackground(new Color(52, 211, 153)); // Place components into specified geographic regions add(btnNorth, BorderLayout.NORTH); add(btnSouth, BorderLayout.SOUTH); add(btnEast, BorderLayout.EAST); add(btnWest, BorderLayout.WEST); add(btnCenter, BorderLayout.CENTER); addWindowListener(new WindowAdapter() { public void windowClosing(WindowEvent e) { System.exit(0); } }); setSize(480, 300); setLocationRelativeTo(null); setVisible(true); } public static void main(String[] args) { new FiveRegionBorderLayout(); } } Layout Mechanics: NORTH and SOUTH stretch across the entire horizontal span while respecting their preferred vertical heights. title: Write a program that uses MouseListener to display messages when the mouse is clicked, entered, and exited over a Panel.
chunks: The program below registers a MouseListener on a specialized canvas/panel to capture and report mouse cursor interactions: import java.awt.*; import java.awt.event.*; public class PanelMouseTracker extends Frame implements MouseListener { private Panel sensorPanel; private Label lblFeedback; public PanelMouseTracker() { setTitle("Panel Mouse Interaction Tracker"); setLayout(new BorderLayout(8, 8)); sensorPanel = new Panel(); sensorPanel.setBackground(new Color(30, 41, 59)); // Slate background lblFeedback = new Label("Move mouse over the box or click inside it", Label.CENTER); // Attach MouseListener to the sub-container sensorPanel.addMouseListener(this); add(sensorPanel, BorderLayout.CENTER); add(lblFeedback, BorderLayout.SOUTH); addWindowListener(new WindowAdapter() { public void windowClosing(WindowEvent e) { System.exit(0); } }); setSize(420, 260); setVisible(true); } @Override public void mouseClicked(MouseEvent e) { sensorPanel.setBackground(new Color(52, 211, 153)); // Green on click lblFeedback.setText("Mouse CLICKED at (" + e.getX() + ", " + e.getY() + ")! Click count: " + e.getClickCount()); } @Override public void mouseEntered(MouseEvent e) { sensorPanel.setBackground(new Color(56, 189, 248)); // Blue on enter lblFeedback.setText("Mouse ENTERED the panel area."); } @Override public void mouseExited(MouseEvent e) { sensorPanel.setBackground(new Color(30, 41, 59)); // Restore slate lblFeedback.setText("Mouse EXITED the panel area."); } // Unused methods satisfied for interface contract public void mousePressed(MouseEvent e) {} public void mouseReleased(MouseEvent e) {} public static void main(String[] args) { new PanelMouseTracker(); } }

Interaction Lifecycle & Coordinate Feedback Moving the mouse cursor over the dark sensor panel triggers mouseEntered() , turning the panel background bright blue. Moving outside triggers mouseExited() , restoring the dark background. Clicking inside the panel invokes mouseClicked() , which retrieves precise coordinates via e.getX() and e.getY() and flashes the panel green. The MouseEvent object also provides e.getClickCount() to distinguish between single-clicks and double-clicks, and e.getButton() to identify left versus right mouse button clicks.

title: Create a GUI with a TextArea and a Clear button. Clear the text area when the button is clicked.
chunks: The application below provides a multi-line note editor featuring a reset/clear mechanism that blanks the TextArea and returns focus: import java.awt.*; import java.awt.event.*; public class TextEditorClearDemo extends Frame implements ActionListener { private TextArea textArea; private Button btnClear; private Label lblCharCount; public TextEditorClearDemo() { setTitle("Scratchpad & Text Reset Utility"); setLayout(new BorderLayout(8, 8)); textArea = new TextArea("Type initial notes here... Line 2 Line 3", 8, 30); btnClear = new Button("Clear All Text"); lblCharCount = new Label("Characters: 43"); btnClear.addActionListener(this); Panel bottomPanel = new Panel(new FlowLayout()); bottomPanel.add(btnClear); bottomPanel.add(lblCharCount); add(new Label("Enter your notes below:", Label.CENTER), BorderLayout.NORTH); add(textArea, BorderLayout.CENTER); add(bottomPanel, BorderLayout.SOUTH); addWindowListener(new WindowAdapter() { public void windowClosing(WindowEvent e) { System.exit(0); } }); pack(); setLocationRelativeTo(null); setVisible(true); } @Override public void actionPerformed(ActionEvent e) { // Reset text area content to empty string textArea.setText(""); lblCharCount.setText("Characters: 0 (Cleared!)"); // Return keyboard focus to the text area for immediate typing textArea.requestFocus(); } public static void main(String[] args) { new TextEditorClearDemo(); } } Technical Detail: Calling textArea.setText("") clears both displayed characters and internal buffer, while requestFocus() provides superior UX by positioning the blinking cursor back inside the editor.

Buffer Management & Cursor Positioning A TextArea maintains an internal character buffer. Invoking textArea.setText("") clears all lines of text and resets the scrollbars to top position. Calling textArea.requestFocus() immediately directs hardware keyboard focus back to the editor, ensuring the user can begin typing immediately without clicking. In real-world text editors, the clear operation is often paired with an 'Undo' buffer or a confirmation dialog to prevent accidental data loss when resetting extensive notes. This ensures seamless and responsive interaction during long editing sessions.

title: Write a program using KeyListener to show a message when the Enter key is pressed.
chunks: The program below intercepts low-level keyboard strokes using KeyListener and detects the virtual key constant KeyEvent.VK_ENTER : import java.awt.*; import java.awt.event.*; public class EnterKeyDetector extends Frame implements KeyListener { private TextField txtCommand; private Label lblStatus; public EnterKeyDetector() { setTitle("Enter Key Press Detector"); setLayout(new GridLayout(3, 1, 8, 8)); Label lblPrompt = new Label("Type a command and press ENTER:", Label.CENTER); txtCommand = new TextField(25); lblStatus = new Label("Status: Waiting for Enter key...", Label.CENTER); // Register KeyListener on the text field txtCommand.addKeyListener(this); add(lblPrompt); add(txtCommand); add(lblStatus); addWindowListener(new WindowAdapter() { public void windowClosing(WindowEvent e) { System.exit(0); } }); setSize(380, 160); setVisible(true); } @Override public void keyPressed(KeyEvent e) { // Intercept VK_ENTER virtual key code if (e.getKeyCode() == KeyEvent.VK_ENTER) { String text = txtCommand.getText().trim(); lblStatus.setText("ENTER Pressed! Executing command: '" + text + "'"); txtCommand.selectAll(); } } public void keyReleased(KeyEvent e) {} public void keyTyped(KeyEvent e) {} public static void main(String[] args) { new EnterKeyDetector(); } } Why keyPressed() is preferred over keyTyped() : Non-character functional keys (Enter, Esc, F1-F12, Shift, Ctrl) generate keyPressed and keyReleased with a valid e.getKeyCode() , but may not trigger keyTyped() .

Virtual Key Constants & Command Execution Flow The KeyEvent class provides virtual key constants ( VK_* ) representing hardware keyboard keys independent of language layout. Comparing e.getKeyCode() == KeyEvent.VK_ENTER allows instant form submission or command dispatch without requiring the user to manually click a submit button. The Enter key also generates an ActionEvent directly on TextField components, allowing developers to choose between high-level action events or low-level key events depending on application requirements.

Create MenuBar container MenuBar menuBar = new MenuBar(); // 2. Create "File" dropdown menu Menu menuFile = new Menu("File"); // 3. title: Build a GUI containing a List of subjects and a button that displays the selected subject.
chunks: An AWT List provides a scrollable multi-line list box. The following program enables subject selection and prints the active choice upon clicking a confirmation button: import java.awt.*; import java.awt.event.*; public class SubjectListSelector extends Frame implements ActionListener { private List listSubjects; private Button btnSelect; private Label lblResult; public SubjectListSelector() { setTitle("Subject Selection Catalog"); setLayout(new FlowLayout(FlowLayout.CENTER, 15, 15)); Label lblPrompt = new Label("Choose a subject from the list:"); // List with 4 visible rows; false indicates single-selection mode listSubjects = new List(4, false); listSubjects.add("Design and Analysis of Algorithms"); listSubjects.add("Object Oriented Programming with Java"); listSubjects.add("Relational Database Management Systems"); listSubjects.add("Operating System Principles"); listSubjects.add("Discrete Mathematics & Graph Theory"); btnSelect = new Button("Confirm Selection"); lblResult = new Label("Selected: [None]"); btnSelect.addActionListener(this); add(lblPrompt); add(listSubjects); add(btnSelect); add(lblResult); addWindowListener(new WindowAdapter() { public void windowClosing(WindowEvent e) { System.exit(0); } }); setSize(420, 240); setVisible(true); } @Override public void actionPerformed(ActionEvent e) { String selected = listSubjects.getSelectedItem(); if (selected == null) { lblResult.setText("Warning: Please click a subject first!"); } else { lblResult.setText("Selected: " + selected + " (Index: " + listSubjects.getSelectedIndex() + ")"); } } public static void main(String[] args) { new SubjectListSelector(); } }

List Selection Mechanics & Multiple Selection Modes The AWT List component supports both single-selection ( multipleMode = false ) and multi-selection ( multipleMode = true ). With single-selection active, clicking a subject highlights that row exclusively. Invoking listSubjects.getSelectedItem() retrieves the active string, while getSelectedIndex() provides its 0-based integer position. For multi-select lists, getSelectedItems() returns an array of Strings, while getSelectedIndexes() returns an array of primitive integer positions. The choice between single and multiple selection modes is configured at component creation.

title: Analyze why an ActionListener may not respond to a button click. Identify two likely coding errors and show how to correct them.
chunks: In Java's Delegation Event Model, an ActionListener failing to respond to button clicks is a classic runtime defect. Two primary coding errors and their diagnostic fixes are detailed below:

Defect 1: Missing Listener Registration (Unwired Observer) Analysis: The button is instantiated and added to the layout, and the class implements ActionListener with a valid actionPerformed() method. However, the programmer omitted the registration statement button.addActionListener(this) . The AWT EventQueue generates the ActionEvent on click, but finds an empty listener collection in the button peer, dropping the event with no error message. // FAULTY CODE: Button btnSubmit = new Button("Submit"); add(btnSubmit); // Button visible on screen, but deaf to clicks! // RESOLUTION: btnSubmit.addActionListener(this); // Registers callback with event source

Defect 2: Faulty Source or ActionCommand Filtering in actionPerformed Analysis: In classes listening to multiple controls, actionPerformed() frequently filters events via e.getSource() or e.getActionCommand() . Comparing strings using reference equality == instead of .equals() , or comparing against the wrong button reference, causes the entire conditional block to evaluate to false silently. // FAULTY CODE: public void actionPerformed(ActionEvent e) { if (e.getActionCommand() == "Submit") { // BUG: '==' checks pointer address, NOT string content! updateLabel(); } } // RESOLUTION: Use .equals() or check object references via e.getSource(): public void actionPerformed(ActionEvent e) { if ("Submit".equals(e.getActionCommand()) || e.getSource() == btnSubmit) { updateLabel(); } }

Diagnostic Debugging Strategies When an action event fails to trigger, developers should place diagnostic print statements inside actionPerformed() : System.out.println("Event fired from: " + e.getActionCommand()); . If this line does not print to the console when clicked, listener registration was omitted. If it prints but the GUI doesn't update, the issue lies in variable shadowing or condition logic.

title: Compare FlowLayout, BorderLayout, and GridLayout for a student registration window. Select a suitable layout for each part and justify your choice.

Layout Manager Key Characteristics Role in Student Registration Window Design Justification BorderLayout Divides window into 5 zones (North, South, East, West, Center). Outer regions stretch. Center Form Fields Panel (e.g., 4x2) Guarantees exact pairwise alignment: labels in column 0 match up flawlessly with corresponding input fields in column 1.
